latin.2353: XXXIV. Igitur, ex mente Doctorum istorum, Gratia excitans consistit in mentis quadam illuminatione, & piis quibusdam cogitationibus, affectibus & desideriis, in hominum animis, non expectato illorum consensu, immediate a Deo excitatis. Ad quae proinde mens & voluntas hominis physice quidem concurrit, quoniam sunt actus vitales, a facultatibus illis profluentes, sed tamen non libere: quia sunt actus indeliberati, qui mentis consultationem, & electionem voluntatis praeveniunt.
latin.2354: XXXV. Gratia vero adjuvans, ex eorundem Doctorum sententia, praecipue consistit in dono & auxilio quodam ordinis supernaturalis, quo voluntas elevatur, & juvatur ad eliciendos actus, qui naturales ejus vires superant. Quod auxilium voluntatem movet physice atque effective: sed tamen non concurrit ad opus supernaturale prius natura, quam liberum arbitrium: neque se habet proprie, ut causa totalis, respectu actus supernaturalis, sed ut causa partialis duntaxat.
latin.2355: XXXVI. Qui autem distinctius enumerant ea in quibus gratia illa excitans consistit, ad eam referunt, primo internam quandam auditionem, & praeconceptionem veritatum fidei, quae assensum antecedit. Deinde coruscationes quasdam divinas, quibus ita derepente percellitur mens nostra, ut nova quadam & inusitata luce experiamur nos cognoscere & intueri magnitudinem & dignitatem rerum divinarum; aut etiam foeditatem peccatorum, & exiguitatem rerum humanarum, & alia ejusmodi, quae attentius animadversa, atque considerata, vehementer hominem movent, ut ad Deum se totum convertat.
latin.2356: XXXVII. In hoc genere quoque ponunt interiorem quandam delectationem in voluntate, ex ejusmodi illustrationibus sequi solitam. Et praeterea varios motus qui divinitus excitantur in appetitu: qualia sunt amor, timor, spes, dolor, & confusio, & similes affectiones, quibus trahitur, & inclinatur interdum ratio superior, ut virtutem sectetur, & declinet vitia.
latin.2357: XXXVIII. Imo quanquam auxilium illud speciale, quod in excitans & adjuvans dividunt, in internis animi motibus, ut dictum est, proprie consistat; multi tamen ad gratiam excitantem revocant etiam externa quaedam: ut sunt occasiones & opportunitates, quas divina providentia suppeditat homini, ut in eo excitentur hujusmodi motus, tam in intellectu, quam in appetitu. Cujusmodi sunt infirmitas, pericula, boni socii, adversitates, & alii varii eventus: sicut videre est apud Gregorium de Valentia loco modo citato. Et similiter Alvares notat gratiam excitantem comprehendere excitationem, tum externam, quae fit per creaturas & signa sensibilia; tum etiam internam, quae fit a Deo immediate, quum immittit pias cogitationes, & proponit ea quae inducere possunt liberum arbitrium ad actum fidei & charitatis, & alias supernaturales operationes. De auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 8. disp. 75.
latin.2358: XXXIX. Verum alii Scholae Romanae Theologi distinctionem gratiae in excitantem atque adjuvantem diverso plane modo exponunt atque intelligunt. Patet enim ex dictis, juxta priores illos, gratiam excitantem esse, per quam homo excitatur & sollicitatur ad bonum, licet illud nondum velit: adjuvantem autem esse, per quam homo adjuvatur ut velit, ac deinde faciat. Quo referunt illud Apocalypseos, Ecce ego sto ad ostium & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, &c. Sed posteriores isti de quibus jam agimus, locum illum de gratia excitante non exponendum esse censent. Dicunt enim non esse idem pulsare & excitare. Quoniam multis adhibetur pulsatio, tum per externum ministerium praedicationis, exhortationis & increpationis, tum per internas illustrationes & inspirationes, qui tamen a somno peccati, vel negligentiae non excitantur, neque evigilant, sed consopiti manent, qui proinde nondum dici possunt excitantem gratiam habere. Quemadmodum & iis accidit, qui corporis somno detinentur, ut pulsatione adhibita, non tamen statim expergiscantur.
latin.2359: XL. Igitur per gratiam excitantem intelligunt illam qua homini peccatori, aut a bono opere cessanti, & tanquam quodam sopore depresso, ita immittitur cogitatio, desiderium, & voluntas boni operis, ut jam vere excitatus a somno peccati, aut negligentiae bonorum operum dici possit. Gratiam vero adjuvantem vocant illam qua is qui jam est excitatus adjuvatur, ut perfectius velit quod jam velle incepit: utque perficiat quod jam voluit. Excitat enim, inquiunt, gratia ut velimus, adjuvat ut faciamus. Excitantis gratiae est velle; adjuvantis facere atque perficere. Quae interpretatio est Gulielmi Estii in lib. 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. undecimo.
latin.2360: XLI. Eodem modo istam gratiae partitionem in excitantem atque adjuvantem explicat Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis, de gratia Christi salvatoris libro quarto capite decimo sexto. Quemadmodum, inquit, haec proprie vocatur Excitans, quae bonum voluntatis motum in potentia voluntatis excitat, ubi non erat nisi malus, vel quae excitat potentiam voluntatis mortuam sopitamque Deo, ut accepto bene volendi motu, incipiat vivere & vigilare; ita Adjuvans illa proprie ab Augustino & Patribus vocatur, quae jam excitato acceptoque bonae voluntatis motu, hominem jam volentem conantemque adjuvat, ut vel efficiat quod voluerit, vel ut fortius velit quod velle coepit, carnisque concupiscentiam acceptae voluntati pertinacissime resistentem superet. Quod ut clarius explicet, in praecedentibus docet, in ista divisione excitationem gratiae non tam esse quamlibet provocationem, vel incitationem ad actum, quam primam suscitationem, seu excitationem, sive emicationem sopitae, mortuae extinctaeque volitionis bonae.
latin.2361: XLII. In Scholis quoque Romanis trita & celeberrima est gratiae divisio in Operantem, & Cooperantem. Quae sumpta est ex verbis Augustini, in libro de Gratia & libero Arbitrio capite decimo septimo. Ipse, inquit, ut velimus operatur incipiens, qui volentibus cooperatur perficiens. Et paulo post, ut velimus, inquit, sine nobis operatur. Quum autem volumus, & sic volumus, ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur. Adeoque juxta communem & confusam quandam notionem, Gratia Operans dicitur, quae sola sine nobis operatur. Cooperans vero, quae non operatur sine nobis, sed cui cooperamur.
latin.2362: XLIII. Sed non convenit inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae, quae sit illa gratia quae sine nobis operatur: & etiam quae sit illa quae nobis cooperatur, & quomodo, & quatenus illi cooperemur. Vetustiores Scholastici, testante Bellarmino, gratiam Operantem vocant ipsum habitum gratiae, ut formaliter nos justos & gratos Deo reddit, Id enim Deus in nobis, sine nobis facit. Gratiam cooperantem esse volunt eundem habitum, ut operis meritorii principium est. Quum enim bona opera facimus, non sola gratia operatur in nobis: sed & nos ipsi vere cooperamur.
latin.2363: XLIV. Verum hodierni plerique Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, per gratiam operantem intelligunt, eam per quam in nobis producuntur illi animi motus, qui sunt indeliberati, & a Libero consensu voluntatis nostrae non pendent. Quales sunt piae cogitationes, & mentis illustrationes, & etiam pia quaedam desideria, quibus a Deo movemur atque sollicitamur ad fidem & conversionem.
latin.2364: XLV. Ac monent hanc gratiam recte dici in nobis, sine nobis operari, non quod mens & voluntas nostra mere passive se habeant ad motus illos quos in nobis producit: Cum enim sint motus vitales, a potentia vitali, inquiunt, efficienter procedere debent: sed quia per illam Deus in nobis operatur, sine nobis moraliter, seu libere concurrentibus; licet non sine nobis Physice operantibus. Non enim, ut aiunt, illae actiones nobis tribui solent, quae fiunt sine libertate, quaeque dicuntur actiones hominis; sed eae duntaxat ad quas nos libere determinamus, & quae proprie actiones humanae appellantur.
latin.2365: XLVI. Consequenter autem per gratiam cooperantem intelligunt illam quae in nobis producit liberum illum voluntatis consensum, quo vocationi divinae obsequimur, aliosque deinceps voluntatis nostrae actus, quibus in bono pergimus, magisque ac magis ad Deum convertimur. Illam vero vocari dicunt non operantem, sed cooperantem, quoniam libere cum ea concurrimus; nec actus illi qui ei tribuuntur, a sola gratia procedunt, sed etiam a nostro libero Arbitrio.
latin.2366: XLVII. Itaque quod dicit Augustinus, gratiam sine nobis operari ut Velimus, intelligunt de actu voluntatis indeliberato, & de imperfecto quodam desiderio. Quod autem addit, Quum Volumus nobiscum cooperatur, intelligunt de actu voluntatis consummato, & de electione perfecta & deliberata. Et sic gratiam operantem & cooperantem exponunt communiter hodie Jesuitae, & plurimi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui a partibus eorum stant contra Dominicanos & Thomistas recentiores. Ut videre est apud Becanum libello de Auxiliis Gratiae juxta Catholicos, qui liber est inter ejus opuscula. Et Petrum a sancto Joseph in Idea Theologiae speculativae, lib. 4. cap. 6. Resolutione 4.
latin.2367: XLVIII. Quibus consentanea docet Gabriel Vasquez, nempe gratiam operantem esse ipsam sanctam cogitationem, quae est ante consensum, atque eodem modo motum voluntatis subitum, sine nostra libertate ex pia illa cogitatione ortum, quo deterremur a malo & ad bonum provocamur: gratiam vero cooperantem esse in consensu libero, in quo jam meritum aliquod reperitur, sive vitae aeternae condignum, sive impetratorium alicujus doni. Deum enim in nobis sine nobis operari sanctam cogitationem, & primum motum voluntatis non deliberatum, quae duo sunt initium bonae operationis & salutis nostrae: at consensum ipsum, quem huic vocationi praebemus, Deum operari nobiscum. in 1. Thom. to. 1. Disput. 88. cap. 6. num. 20.
latin.2368: XLIX. Caeterum Andreas Vega, inter Doctores illos qui Concilio Tridentino interfuerunt non parum celebris, eadem quidem, quae jam dicti Doctores, ad gratiam operantem refert, nempe sanctam cogitationem & primum motum voluntatis, quo homo subito movetur ad bonum. Sed censet alia de causa Deum dici ista in nobis sine nobis operari. Nimirum quia ad istius motus, & sanctae istius cogitationis productionem, Deus solus physice operatur, homo autem passive omnino se habet; In eo siquidem hominem non solum non agere libere, sed nequidem physice actionem ullam elicere. Quod autem istum Doctorem impulit ut ita sentiret, illud est, quod cum Scholasticis illis, qui Mominales appellantur, existimavit in homine a solo Deo efficiente posse produci intellectionem, & volitionem aliquam, intellectu & voluntate omnino patiente, nec agente ullo modo, etiamsi illa qualitate homo informatus intelligere & velle dicatur: quia licet ista grammatice ut actiones hominis exprimantur, non sunt tamen revera, in eo casu, actiones & productiones mentis & voluntatis, sed solum qualitates, quae suo effectu formali reddunt hominem intelligentem & volentem, qua de re videndus Vasquez disputationis modo citatae cap. 3.
latin.2369: L. At vero sunt alii qui per gratiam operantem designari putant eam, quae efficit in homine primum actum deliberatae voluntatis: qualis est conversio, sive ab infidelitate ad fidem, sive a peccatis caeteris ad poenitentiam. Per gratiam vero cooperantem intelligunt illam quae efficit consequentes actus voluntatis: quales sunt velle orare, velle bona opera facere, & alii similes. Ita ut gratia operans nihil sit aliud quam auxilium speciale efficax respectu primi actus voluntatis: gratia vero cooperans sit auxilium speciale efficax quoque, respectu actuum sequentium.
latin.2370: LI. Haec est sententia Bellarmini, qui pertendit merito posse dici Deum operari in nobis, sine nobis, primum illud Velle deliberatum, quo ad Deum convertimur: licet non tantum physice, sed etiam libere a voluntate nostra eliciatur. Nam, inquit, si consideremus causam efficientem illius actus, ea non solum est Deus per auxilium speciale; sed etiam voluntas per liberum arbitrium; & hoc modo Deus illum operatur non sine nobis. At si consideremus causam ejusdem actus moralem, id est, causam suadendo, hortando, consulendo, ea solus est Deus. Non enim ipsa se voluntas impellit suadendo, & hortando, ut velit quod non vult; sed Deus per inspirationes suas intus animae loquens, ei suadet, & persuadet ut velit. Igitur, juxta illum, gratia operans est, quae praevenit conatum & industriam nostram, & operatur ut velimus quod antea nolebamus, sine nobis operantibus ut velimus; non tamen sine nobis libere consentientibus, dum volumus.
latin.2371: LII. Gratia autem illa quae requiritur ad reliquos actus voluntatis, post primum, ex ejus sententia, dicitur cooperans, quoniam postea quam coepimus converti ad Deum, jam nos ipsi non tantum per liberum arbitrium producimus, Deo juvante, reliquos actus; sed etiam nos incitamus & impellimus, Deo cooperante, ad eos. Itaque, inquit, gratia operans est quae facit nos velle credere; quia id in nobis fit, sine nobis petentibus, ac multo minus laborantibus & conantibus: Et gratia cooperans, quae facit nos velle orare, jejunare, & eleemosynas dare: quia id non fit nisi conatu, & industria nostra cooperante. Unde colligit Deum non operari velle nostrum sine nobis; sed tantum operari ut velimus sine nobis: quoniam scilicet, Deo cooperamur volendo, id est, libere producendo actum volendi; sed non cooperamur faciendo ut velimus. Quia non ipsi nos movemus & incitamus ad volendum: sed ipse solus interna inspiratione nos movet atque impellit.
latin.2372: LIII. Eodem recidit quod docet Estius, Gratiam operantem vulgo dici in nobis sine nobis operari, quoniam primus conversionis actus, seu primus bonus voluntatis motus, qui ejus gratiae effectus est, a voluntate quidem est, tanquam a principio activo & libero; sed tamen Deus illum per gratiam suam operatur, sine praevio in nobis alio motu voluntatis, quo ad primum illum motum conemur, aut aspiremus, aut quo voluntas eum sibi imperet. Quippe cum interdum homini, etiam valde repugnanti, inspiretur bonus affectus voluntatis, ut in Paulo contigit. Cujus conversio, quantum attinet ad mutationem illam ex malo in bonum factam per gratiam operantem, forma est & exemplar conversionis omnium peccatorum. Quoniam per Dei gratiam ex aversis convertuntur & ex nolentibus volentes redduntur. Reliquos vero voluntatis actus, qui primum illum consequuntur, & quibus Deo pergimus adhaerere, gratia Dei quidem operatur quoq; in nobis; sed tamen voluntas nostra ad Deum jam conversa, non solum illos libere producit, verum etiam per alios anteriores actus sibi imperat. Et ita modo quodam singulari cooperatur divinae gratiae, quae propterea hoc respectu dicitur cooperans. In 2. Sentent. Dist. 26. §. 11.
latin.2373: LIV. Non dissimili modo Gratiam operantem & cooperantem explicat Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis. Gratia, inquit, operans est illa quae sola sine studio, sine oratione, sine merito hominis praecedente, voluntatem, seu velle operatur, per quod voluntas ex mala fit bona, & ex injusta justa. Cooperans vero quae homini jam volenti, conantique cooperatur, firmam illam augendo roborandoque voluntatem, ut id efficiat & perficiat quod voluerit & conatur. Ibidemque ex Augustino docet gratiam operantem esse, qua cum ante nollemus, efficitur ut velimus: cooperantem, qua quando jam actu volumus, efficitur ut fortius velimus, ita ut superando quaevis obstacula, etiam reipsa faciamus. Illam operari ut quoquomodo voluntatem bonam, seu velle bonum habeamus: hanc ut illa bona voluntas augeatur & roboretur. Unde colligit cooperantem gratiam nunquam dici respectu primae voluntatis bonae, quando in eam erumpit potentia voluntatis, quoniam illa prima voluntas, seu volitio bona, est solius gratiae operantis effectus, sed solum respectu bonae voluntatis postquam homo jam velle coepit, ut illud velle perseveret, augeatur, bonisque operibus velut fructibus cumuletur.
latin.2374: LV. Gratia operans igitur, ut diligenter observat, sola primam bonam voluntatem in homine efficit, non quod homo non simul in illam voluntatem, hoc est, in voluntatis motum atque consensionem influat, sed quia motum illum gratia operatur, nobis nihil ad eum habendum conferentibus, petendo, desiderando, studendo, meditando, atque ita nihil omnino boni meriti, respectu illius voluntatis, afferendo. Illud enim impossibile esse, hoc ipso quo statuitur, esse prima voluntas bona, ad quam ex mala convertitur. Vicissim vero gratia cooperans sic dicta est, quia operatur aliquid in nobis non sola, sed nobis simul cooperantibus; non per simultaneum tantum influxum, quo etiam cooperamur gratiae operanti, sed praevie ad effectum istius gratiae, Volendo, credendo, desiderando, petendo, pulsando, satagendo, adeoque etiam promerendo; ita ut ejus gratiae cooperantis effectus sit universum primae voluntatis illius bonae incrementum, usque ad apicem perfectionis humanae. De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 4. cap. 15.
latin.2375: LVI. Ab his omnibus differt sententia Didaci Alvares. Existimat enim ille ad quamcunque piam operationem, sive sit interior, sive sit exterior; sive sit prima illa qua ad Deum convertimur, sive quaelibet alia eam sequens, semper concurrere gratiam operantem, & gratiam cooperantem. Et quidem gratiam operantem esse, per quam Deus Physice praedeterminat voluntatem nostram ad consensum in quodvis bonum opus: cooperantem vero, per quam Deus quamlibet actionem piam nobiscum operatur. Utrumque enim necessarium esse, & ut Deus praemoveat liberum nostrum arbitrium Physice & efficienter ad quemvis actum supernaturalem; & ut concurrat cum eodem libero arbitrio, quod jam a Deo praemotum se movet ad bonum opus. Gratiam autem operantem dici in ordine ad primum effectum, respectu cujus voluntas nostra solum se habet, ut mota: cooperantem vero, in ordine ad secundum, in quo mota se movet. Idque quoniam voluntas nostra in ordine ad motionem praeviam, qua movetur a Deo ad actus supernaturales, habet se passive, cum talis motio non producatur active a nostro libero arbitrio, sed solum a Deo, a quo est auxilium illud operantis gratiae. Et rursus voluntas mota a Deo producit active & libere operationes supernaturales, cum gratia Dei concurrente. Ac proinde gratia Dei, priore illo respectu, operatur sine nobis: posteriore vero illi cooperamur. De Auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 9. Disp. 81.
latin.2376: LVII. Hic autem quaerunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, quomodo Gratia operans distinguatur ab excitante: & gratia cooperans a gratia adjuvante. Sed ex jam dictis facile colligi potest quid ad hanc quaestionem, juxta uniuscujusque placita, respondendum sit. Etenim illi qui, cum Vasquezio, Molina, & plerisque Jesuitis, per gratiam excitantem intelligunt tantum gratiam Pulsantem & Sollicitantem, & quidem saepe frustra: per gratiam vero Adjuvantem, illam qua Deus concurrit auxilio speciali cum libero arbitrio, dum gratiae consentit, & ei obsequitur: Ac rursus per gratiam operantem, illam quae in nobis efficit pias cogitationes, & motus indeliberatos, ad quos Physice quidem, sed non libere concurrimus; per cooperantem vero, illam quae in nobis producit liberos voluntatis actus, quibus Deo vocanti & invitanti respondemus; illi, inquam, existimant gratiam operantem eandem esse cum excitante, & gratiam adjuvantem eandem cum cooperante. Nempe juxta illos, eadem gratia, & dicitur excitans, quatenus per sanctas cogitationes, & desideria pia nobis immissa nos sollicitat & excitat ad bonum; Et operans, quatenus ista in nobis operatur, sine nobis libere concurrentibus, & consentientibus. Et similiter eadem gratia & adjuvans dicitur, quatenus nos adjuvat, dum invitanti gratiae consentimus; Et cooperans, quatenus non operatur sine nobis libere nostrum consensum praebentibus.
latin.2377: LVIII. Eodem modo gratia excitans eadem est cum operante, & gratia adjuvans eadem cum cooperante, omnibus illis, qui cum Jansenio & Estio per gratiam excitantem intelligunt illam, quae revera excitat peccatorem a somno peccati, & per adjuvantem illam qua homo adjuvatur, ut perficiat bonum quod jam velle incepit: Ac per operantem eam quae in nobis efficit primum conversionis actum, per cooperantem eam quae alios sequentes, ad quos non tantum libero quodam voluntatis influxu, sed etiam praevio aliquo studio & conatu nostro cooperamur.
latin.2378: LIX. Sed qui, cum Jansenio & Estio, volunt quidem gratiam operantem dici, quae in nobis operatur primam conversionem; & cooperantem, quae nos movet ad bona opera quae inde consequuntur: sed pertendunt cum Jesuitis gratiam excitantem esse, qua pulsamur ut a somno vitiorum evigilemus, etiamsi culpa nostra sopiti saepe maneamus; adjuvantem vero quae nos roborat & adjuvat, dum somnum istum revera excutimus: illi, inquam, ut Bellarminus, gratiam excitantem ab operante distinguunt, & consequenter gratiam adjuvantem a cooperante: Nam illis gratia excitans latius patet quam operans. Adeoque gratiam excitantem dividunt in sufficientem atque efficacem. Et rursus efficacem in operantem & cooperantem, ut videre est apud eundem Bellarminum libro 1. de Gratia saepius jam citato.
latin.2379: LX. Similiter Alvares gratiam excitantem distinguit ab operante: quoniam gratia excitans ipsi est gratia quaedam voluntatem ad bonum moraliter tantum trahens & alliciens. Operans vero, gratia non solum moraliter, sed etiam physice voluntatem ad bonum praemovens & praedeterminans. Adeoque, juxta ipsum, gratia excitans eadem est cum gratia sufficiente. Gratia vero operans & cooperans pertinent ad gratiam efficacem.
latin.2380: LXI. Sed inter Scholae Romanae Theologos praecipua hic controversia est de modo quo Der gratia cum voluntate nostra cooperatur. Etenim Jesuitae, & alii complures Scholae Romanae Doctores, negant gratiam adjuvantem, sive cooperantem prius natura concurrere ad opus supernaturale, quam liberum arbitrium; Et hoc ne admittant, gratiam praedeterminare liberum arbitrium. Unde, ipsorum judicio, periret libertas voluntatis; cui, ex ista hypothesi, gratia divina imponeret aliquam agendi necessitatem, quae cum libertate consistere non posset. Sic inter alios sentit & ratiocinatur Petrus a sancto Joseph, in idea Theologiae speculativae, libro quarto, capite sexto, ubi sic incipit ejus tertia Resolutio, Gratia adjuvans uon concurrit prius natura ad opus supernaturale, quam liberum arbitrium.
latin.2381: LXII. Contra vero pertendunt alii gratiam adjuvantem atque cooperantem, secundum causalitatis ordinem, praevenire liberum arbitrium, & prius quam illud agere: Ac quanquam simul tempore tam gratia, quam liberum arbitrium influant in piam operationem, natura tamen quodammodo priorem esse gratiae influxum, nec ordine causalitatis cum influxu liberi arbitrii simultaneum. Haec est sententia Didaci Alvares in Epitome de Auxiliis divinae gratiae, libro tertio, capite decimo nono, cujus hoc lemma est, Quod Gratia cooperans, in quantum cooperans, sit praeveniens, seu praemovens liberum arbitrium ad consensum, & non solum pariter, & simultanee cum illo in piam operationem influens. Idem vero caput his verbis incipit, Ex praemissis constat, quod gratia cooperans, quatenus ab excitante distinguitur, sit praeveniens liberam cooperationem arbitrii creati, non quidem prioritate temporis, sed rationis duntaxat & causalitatis.
latin.2382: LXIII. Neque propterea quicquam praejudicari putant libertati voluntatis humanae; quoniam gratia Dei sic movet & determinat liberum arbitrium creatum ad agendum, ut ab eo non tollat potestatem aliter agendi: ita ut posita gratia, agat quidem infallibiliter, sed semper in sensu diviso potens sit non agere, aut aliter agere.
latin.2383: LXIV. Praeterea qui Molinae Jesuitae Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, docent gratiam adjuvantem, sive cooperantem non se habere proprie ut causam totalem, respectu actus supernaturalis, sed ut causam partialem duntaxat. Et hoc quia gratia adjuvans, ex eorum sententia, non producit actum supernaturalem, nisi dependenter a Libero arbitrio.
latin.2384: LXV. Admittunt quidem totum actum supernaturalem a gratia pendere: verum addunt illum non pendere ab ea totaliter, sed partialiter tantum: quia gratia, scilicet, nequit illum producere, nisi dependenter a concursu voluntatis. Ac proinde gratiam posse quidem dici causam totalem actus boni totalitate effectus, sed non totalitate causae, de qua hic agitur: quoniam totus quidem effectus a gratia pendet, sed tamen ut a causa quae illum non producit sine alia causa concurrente, & simul cum ea agente. Unde est quod comparant gratiam & liberum arbitrium duobus equis currum eundem simul trahentibus, quorum neuter altero prius agit, & alterum movet ad agendum, & qui tractionis illius sunt causae tantum partiales; licet tota tractio dici possit, ab equis singulis dependere, quia singuli ad totam tractionem aliquid conferunt.
latin.2385: LXVI. Itaque ex eorum mente, gratia adjuvans ut sic & praecise considerata, non movet hominem ad agendum, sed illum juvat in actuali operatione. Gratia excitans vero, etsi hominem moveat ad agendum, non tamen illi imponit agendi necessitatem; sed illi suas partes relinquit, ut se nimirum determinet ad opus pium, cum alioqui possit ab eo abstinere, si velit, & aliter se determinare. Unde nec illa dici debet causa totalis, sive adaequata bonae operationis, ut videre est apud eundem Petrum a sancto Joseph loco supra citato.
latin.2386: LXVII. Contra vero Estius & Thomistae recentiores docent gratiam Dei ita esse totalem causam boni operis, ut quicquid est in opere boni totum faciat, & totum opus sit gratiae divinae ascribendum, tanquam causae totali, non solum tanquam partiali.
latin.2387: LXVIII. Sed quamvis absolute & proprie loquendo, asserant totum bonum opus esse a gratia Dei, nihilominus docent idem bonum opus totum esse a libero etiam arbitrio. Quia nihil prohibet aliquid totum esse a duabus causis, quarum una sit alteri subordinata: sic nimirum ut inferior causa omnem suam operandi virtutem, omnemq; motum accipiat a superiore. Atque hoc docent perpetuum esse in causa prima, & causa secunda; qualiscunque demum sit causa secunda, sive libere agat, sive naturaliter, quia, scilicet, necessarium est, ut quicquid fit a causa secunda referatur ad primam: Nec ullo modo potest in his admitti partitio operum: ut aliquid ulla sui parte existimetur fieri a causa secunda, quod non etiam totum, & omni parte fiat a causa prima applicante causam secundam ad omnem suam operationem.
latin.2388: LXIX. Dicunt igitur totum bonum simul & individuo opere peragi a gratia & libero arbitrio: nec esse distinctum quod est ex libero arbitrio, & quod est ex gratia; quia non est distinctum quod est ex causa prima, & quod est ex causa secunda. Sed inter utrumque agens docent illud esse discrimen, quod liberum arbitrium, sicut suum esse habet a Deo, ita & totum hoc quod bene operatur habet a gratia Dei, in ipso, & per ipsum operantis: non autem contra, vel in totum, vel ex parte, Deus in eo quod operatur, dependet a libero hominis arbitrio. Facit enim Deus ut homo faciat, non autem facit homo ut Deus faciat. Quae eadem ratio est in omni opere, seu actione, quae fit a quacunque causa secunda. Adeoque juxta hos Doctores, gratia divina, & liberum arbitrium non cooperantur ut causae partiales, quae in agendo pendeant ab invicem, sed ut causae totales atque subordinatae, quarum inferior pendet & movetur a superiore, non contra. Ut latius videre est apud eundem Estium in 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. 29.
latin.2389: LXX. Porro cum jam allatis gratiae divisionibus coincidunt aliae quaedam, quae parum aut nihil ab iis differunt. Ut quum gratia dividitur in gratiam praevenientem & in gratiam subsequentem: & in ducentem atque comitantem. Nam per gratiam ducentem atque praevenientem Theologi intelligunt illam eandem quam excitantem & operantem vocant: & per gratiam comitantem sive subsequentem, illam quae alias dicitur adjuvans, sive cooperans. Etenim illa gratia quae nos ad bonum excitat, & eatenus in nobis sine nobis operatur, eadem nos quoque praevenit: quae vero nos adjuvat in actuali operatione, nobisque cooperatur, eadem voluntates nostras in bene agendo censetur comitari, & priorem illam gratiam subsequitur. Nonnulli tamen quaedam subtilia discrimina inter hasce gratiae divisiones quaerunt, sed quae referre & commemorare non multum facit ad nostrum institutum. Quod potissimum hic considerandum restat, est celebris illa gratiae divisio in sufficientem atque efficacem: sed quia accurata ejus expositio res est longioris disquisitionis, in proximam disputationem illam differre visum est.

sections.title: Rousing grace on the first view: enlightenment and stirrings before consent
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. Therefore, in the mind of those Doctors, rousing grace consists in a certain illumination of the mind, and certain pious thoughts, affections and desires, in the souls of men, not waiting for their consent, immediately excited by God. To which therefore the mind and will of man concurs physically indeed, since they are vital acts, flowing from those faculties, but yet not freely: because they are undeliberated acts, which go before the consultation of the mind, and the choice of the will.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIV. On the view of these doctors, then, rousing grace consists in an enlightening of the mind and in devout thoughts, feelings and desires that God stirs up directly in human souls without waiting for their consent.

The human mind and will do take a physical part in these, since they are living acts that come from those faculties. But they do not take part freely, because these are undeliberate acts, which come before the mind has weighed anything and before the will has chosen.

sections.title: Assisting grace on the first view: a partial cause, not prior in nature
sections.pass_a: XXXV. But helping grace, from the opinion of the same Doctors, chiefly consists in a certain gift and help of the supernatural order, by which the will is raised, and helped to elicit acts, which surpass its natural powers. Which help moves the will physically and effectively: but yet does not concur to the supernatural work prior in nature, than free choice: nor does it hold itself properly, as total cause, in respect of the supernatural act, but as partial cause only.
pass_b: Thesis XXXV. Assisting grace, in the opinion of the same doctors, consists chiefly in a gift and help of the supernatural order by which the will is lifted up and helped to produce acts beyond its natural strength.

This help moves the will physically and effectively. Yet it does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature, and with regard to the supernatural act it is not, strictly, the total cause but only a partial one.

sections.title: What rousing grace includes: inner hearing and sudden divine flashes
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. But those who more distinctly enumerate the things in which that rousing grace consists, refer to it, first a certain internal hearing, and preconception of the truths of faith, which goes before assent. Then certain divine flashes, by which our mind is so suddenly struck, that by a certain new and unaccustomed light we experience ourselves to know and behold the greatness and dignity of divine things; or also the foulness of sins, and the smallness of human things, and other things of this kind, which more attentively noticed, and considered, vehemently move man, that he turn himself wholly to God.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVI. Those who list more precisely what this rousing grace consists of include in it, first, an inner hearing and preliminary grasp of the truths of faith, which comes before assent.

Next they include certain divine flashes that strike our mind so suddenly that, in a new and unfamiliar light, we find ourselves knowing and seeing the greatness and worth of divine things, or else the foulness of sin, the smallness of human affairs and the like. When these are noticed and weighed with more attention, they move a person powerfully to turn wholly to God.

sections.title: Delight in the will and movements of the appetite
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. In this kind also they place a certain interior delight in the will, wont to follow from illuminations of this kind. And besides various motions which are divinely excited in the appetite: such as are love, fear, hope, sorrow, and confusion, and like affections, by which the higher reason is drawn, and inclined at times, to follow virtue, and shun vices.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVII. Under this heading they also place an inner delight in the will, which usually follows such enlightenments.

They add various movements that God stirs up in the appetite, such as love, fear, hope, sorrow, shame and similar feelings. By these the higher reason is sometimes drawn and inclined to pursue virtue and turn away from vice.

sections.title: Outward occasions counted as rousing grace (Valencia, Alvarez)
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. Indeed although that special help, which they divide into rousing and helping, consists properly in internal motions of the soul, as has been said; many however refer to rousing grace also certain external things: as are occasions and opportunities, which divine providence supplies to man, that in him motions of this kind may be excited, as well in the intellect, as in the appetite. Of which kind are sickness, dangers, good companions, adversities, and other various events: as is to be seen in Gregory of Valencia in the place just cited. And similarly Alvarez notes that rousing grace comprehends excitation, both external, which happens through creatures and sensible signs; and also internal, which happens from God immediately, when he sends in pious thoughts, and proposes those things which can induce free choice to the act of faith and charity, and other supernatural operations. De auxiliis divinae gratiae book 8 disp. 75.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVIII. Indeed, although that special help, which they divide into rousing and assisting, strictly consists in inward movements of the soul, as has been said, many also count certain outward things as rousing grace. These are the occasions and opportunities that God's providence supplies to a person so that such movements may be stirred in him, in both the intellect and the appetite.
Examples are sickness, dangers, good companions, misfortunes and various other events, as may be seen in Gregory of Valencia at the place just cited.

Alvarez likewise notes that rousing grace includes both an outward rousing, which comes through creatures and signs perceived by the senses, and an inward one, which comes directly from God when he puts devout thoughts into the mind and sets before it what can lead free choice to the act of faith and charity and to other supernatural works (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 8, disputation 75).

sections.title: The second view: knocking is not yet rousing (Revelation 3:20)
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. But other Theologians of the Roman School expound and understand the distinction of grace into rousing and helping in a plainly different way. For it is plain from what has been said, that according to those former ones, rousing grace is that, by which man is roused and solicited to good, although he does not yet will it: but helping is that, by which man is helped that he may will, and then do. To which they refer that of the Apocalypse, Behold I stand at the door and knock, if anyone hears my voice, and opens the door to me, I will come in to him, etc. But these latter of whom we now treat, think that place is not to be expounded of rousing grace. For they say that knocking and rousing are not the same. Since knocking is applied to many, both through the external ministry of preaching, exhortation and rebuke, and through internal illuminations and inspirations, who however are not roused from the sleep of sin, or negligence, nor wake up, but remain fast asleep, who therefore cannot yet be said to have rousing grace. Just as happens also to those who are held by sleep of the body, that when knocking is applied, yet they do not at once wake up.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIX. Other theologians of the Roman school, however, explain and understand the division of grace into rousing and assisting in quite another way. From what has been said it is clear that for the first group rousing grace is the grace by which a person is roused and urged toward good even though he does not yet will it, and assisting grace is the grace by which he is helped to will it and then to do it.
To this they apply the text of Revelation: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will come in to him,' and so on.

The second group, whom we are now discussing, holds that this text should not be taken of rousing grace, because knocking and rousing are not the same thing. Many people are knocked at, both through the outward ministry of preaching, exhortation and rebuke and through inward enlightenments and inspirations, and yet are not roused from the sleep of sin or neglect. They do not wake up but stay sound asleep, and so they cannot yet be said to have rousing grace.
It is the same with people held by bodily sleep: someone knocks, yet they do not wake at once.

sections.title: Estius: rousing grace actually wakes the sinner
sections.pass_a: XL. Therefore by rousing grace they understand that by which to a sinful man, or one ceasing from good work, and as it were weighed down by a certain sleep, thought, desire, and will of a good work is so sent in, that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin, or of negligence of good works. But helping grace they call that by which he who is already roused is helped, that he may will more perfectly what he has already begun to will: and that he may complete what he has already willed. For grace, they say, rouses that we may will, helps that we may do. Of rousing grace it is to will; of helping, to do and to perfect. Which interpretation is of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences distinction 26 paragraph eleven.
pass_b: Thesis XL. By rousing grace, then, they mean the grace by which a sinner, or one who has stopped doing good and lies as if sunk in a kind of sleep, is given the thought, desire and will to do a good work, in such a way that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin or from neglect of good works.
By assisting grace they mean the grace by which someone already roused is helped to will more perfectly what he has begun to will, and to carry out what he has already willed.

'Grace,' they say, 'rouses us to will and assists us to do. Willing belongs to rousing grace; doing and completing belong to assisting grace.' This is the interpretation of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 11.

sections.title: Jansenius on rousing and assisting grace
sections.pass_a: XLI. In the same way Jansenius Bishop of Ypres explains this partition of grace into rousing and helping, on the grace of Christ the saviour in book four chapter sixteen. Just as, he says, that is properly called Rousing, which rouses a good motion of the will in the power of the will, where there was only a bad one, or which rouses the power of the will dead and asleep to God, that having received the motion of willing well, it may begin to live and keep awake; so that is properly called Helping by Augustine and the Fathers, which, the motion of good will being already roused and received, helps the man already willing and striving, that either he may accomplish what he has willed, or that he may will more strongly what he began to will, and may overcome the concupiscence of the flesh most stubbornly resisting the received will. Which that he may explain more clearly, in the preceding he teaches, that in this division the rousing of grace is not so much any provocation, or incitement to act, as the first awakening, or rousing, or flashing forth of the slumbering, dead and extinguished good volition.
pass_b: Thesis XLI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains this division of grace into rousing and assisting in the same way, in book 4, chapter 16 of his treatise on the grace of Christ the Saviour.

'Rousing grace,' he says, 'is properly the grace that stirs up a good movement in the will's power where there was only a bad one, or that wakes the will's power, which is dead and asleep toward God, so that once it has received the movement of willing well it may begin to live and stay awake.

In the same way Augustine and the Fathers properly give the name assisting grace to the grace that, once the movement of good will has been stirred and received, helps the man who already wills and strives, either to carry out what he has willed, or to will more strongly what he has begun to will, and to overcome the desire of the flesh that stubbornly resists the will he has received.'

To explain this more clearly, he teaches in the preceding pages that rousing, in this division, is not so much any urging or prompting to act as the first awakening, rousing or flaring up of a good volition that was asleep, dead and extinguished.

sections.title: Operating and cooperating grace: Augustine's words
sections.pass_a: XLII. In the Roman Schools also the division of grace into Operating, and Cooperating is well-worn and most celebrated. Which is taken from the words of Augustine, in the book on Grace and free Choice chapter seventeen. He himself, he says, that we may will works beginning, who cooperates with those willing perfecting. And a little after, that we may will, he says, he works without us. But when we will, and so will, that we do, he cooperates with us. And so according to a common and somewhat confused notion, Operating Grace is called, that which alone works without us. But cooperating, that which does not work without us, but with which we cooperate.
pass_b: Thesis XLII. In the Roman schools, too, the division of grace into operating and cooperating is familiar and very well known. It is drawn from Augustine's words in On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 17: 'He works at the start, so that we may will; and he cooperates with those who will, to bring the work to completion.' A little later he says: 'He works without us so that we may will; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us.'
So on a common and rather loose understanding, operating grace is the grace that works alone, without us, and cooperating grace is the grace that does not work without us but with which we cooperate.

sections.title: The older scholastics: operating grace as the habit of grace
sections.pass_a: XLIII. But it is not agreed among the Theologians of the Roman Church, what is that grace which works without us: and also what is that which cooperates with us, and how, and how far we cooperate with it. The older Scholastics, as Bellarmine witnesses, call Operating grace the very habit of grace, as it formally renders us just and pleasing to God, For this God does in us, without us. Cooperating grace they will to be the same habit, as it is the principle of meritorious work. For when we do good works, grace does not alone work in us: but we ourselves also truly cooperate.
pass_b: Thesis XLIII. The theologians of the Roman Church, however, do not agree on which grace it is that works without us, or which grace cooperates with us, or how and how far we cooperate with it.

The older scholastics, according to Bellarmine, give the name operating grace to the habit of grace itself, insofar as it formally makes us righteous and pleasing to God, since God does this in us without us. They take cooperating grace to be the same habit insofar as it is the source of meritorious works: when we do good works, grace is not the only thing at work in us, but we ourselves also truly cooperate.

But most present-day Doctors of the Roman Church, by operating grace understand, that through which in us are produced those motions of the soul, which are undeliberated, and do not depend on the free consent of our will. Such are pious thoughts, and illuminations of the mind, and also certain pious desires, by which we are moved by God and solicited to faith and conversion.
pass_b: Thesis XLIV. Most present-day doctors of the Roman Church, however, take operating grace to mean the grace by which those movements of the soul are produced in us that are undeliberate and do not depend on our will's free consent.
These are devout thoughts, enlightenments of the mind and also certain devout desires, by which God moves and urges us toward faith and conversion.

sections.title: 'Without us': not physically passive, but not freely concurring
sections.pass_a: XLV. And they warn that this grace is rightly said to work in us, without us, not because our mind and will hold themselves merely passively to those motions which it produces in us: For since they are vital motions, they must, they say, proceed efficiently from a vital power: but because through it God works in us, without us morally, or freely concurring; though not without us Physically working. For not, as they say, are those actions wont to be attributed to us, which happen without freedom, and which are called actions of man; but only those to which we freely determine ourselves, and which are properly called human actions.
pass_b: Thesis XLV. They point out that this grace is rightly said to work in us without us, not because our mind and will are merely passive toward the movements it produces in us, for since these are living movements they must, they say, come efficiently from a living power.
It is said so rather because by this grace God works in us without our concurring morally, that is, freely, though not without our acting physically.

For, as they say, the actions usually credited to us are not those that happen without freedom, which are called acts of a man, but only those to which we freely determine ourselves, which are properly called human acts.

sections.title: The moderns: cooperating grace produces free consent
sections.pass_a: XLVI. But consequently by cooperating grace they understand that which produces in us that free consent of the will, by which we obey the divine calling, and the other acts of our will thereafter, by which we go on in good, and are more and more turned to God. But they say it is called not operating, but cooperating, since we freely concur with it; nor do those acts which are attributed to it, proceed from grace alone, but also from our free Choice.
pass_b: Thesis XLVI. Accordingly, by cooperating grace they mean the grace that produces in us the free consent of the will by which we obey God's call, and the further acts of our will by which we keep on in good and turn more and more to God.

sections.title: Andres de Vega: man wholly passive, with the Nominalists
sections.pass_a: XLIX. But Andreas Vega, among those Doctors who were present at the Council of Trent not a little famous, refers indeed the same things, which the Doctors just mentioned, to operating grace, namely the holy thought and the first motion of the will, by which man is suddenly moved to good. But he thinks it is for another cause that God is said to work these things in us without us. Namely because for the production of that motion, and of that holy thought, God alone works physically, but man holds himself wholly passively; In it indeed man not only does not act freely, but does not even physically elicit any action. But what drove that Doctor to think so, is this, that with those Scholastics, who are called Nominales, he thought that in man by God alone efficient there can be produced intellection, and some volition, the intellect and will being wholly passive, and not acting in any way, even though man informed by that quality is said to understand and to will: because although these are expressed grammatically as actions of man, they are not however in reality, in that case, actions and productions of the mind and will, but only qualities, which by their formal effect render man understanding and willing, on which matter Vasquez is to be seen in the disputation just cited chap. 3.
pass_b: Thesis XLIX. Andres de Vega, however, a man of no small note among the doctors who attended the Council of Trent, assigns to operating grace the same things as the doctors just named, namely the holy thought and the first movement of the will by which a person is suddenly moved toward good. But he holds that God is said to work these in us without us for a different reason.

His reason is that in producing that movement and that holy thought God alone acts physically, while the man is entirely passive: in it he not only does not act freely, but does not even produce any action physically.

What led this doctor to that view is that, with the scholastics called Nominalists, he thought that God, as sole efficient cause, could produce in a man an act of understanding or of willing while the intellect and will were wholly passive and did nothing at all, even though the man shaped by that quality is said to understand and to will.

Though these are expressed grammatically as a man's actions, in that case they are not really actions or products of the mind and will, but only qualities that by their formal effect make the man understanding and willing. On this see Vasquez, chapter 3 of the disputation just cited.

sections.title: Bellarmine: God alone is the moral cause of the first willing
sections.pass_a: LI. This is the opinion of Bellarmine, who maintains that God can deservedly be said to work in us, without us, that first deliberated Willing, by which we are turned to God; although it is elicited not only physically, but also freely by our will. For, he says, if we consider the efficient cause of that act, it is not only God by special help; but also the will by free choice; and in this way God works it not without us. But if we consider the moral cause of the same act, that is, the cause by persuading, exhorting, counselling, that is God alone. For the will does not itself drive itself by persuading, and exhorting, that it will what it does not will; but God by his inspirations speaking within to the soul, persuades it, and prevails on it that it will. Therefore, according to him, operating grace is, that which goes before our effort and industry, and works that we will what we before did not will, without us working that we will; not however without us freely consenting, while we will.
pass_b: Thesis LI. This is Bellarmine's view. He argues that God can rightly be said to work in us without us that first deliberate act of willing by which we turn to God, even though our will produces it freely and not merely physically.

'If we consider the efficient cause of this act,' he says, 'it is not only God through special help but also the will through free choice, and in this sense God does not work it without us. But if we consider its moral cause, that is, the cause that persuades, urges and advises, that cause is God alone.
For the will does not drive itself by persuading and urging itself to will what it does not will; it is God who, speaking inwardly to the soul by his inspirations, urges and persuades it to will.'

On his view, then, operating grace is the grace that comes before our effort and diligence and brings it about that we will what we did not will before. It does so without our working to make ourselves will, though not without our freely consenting when we will.

sections.title: Bellarmine: cooperating grace for the later acts
sections.pass_a: LII. But that grace which is required for the remaining acts of the will, after the first, according to his opinion, is called cooperating, since after we have begun to be converted to God, now we ourselves not only through free choice produce, God helping, the remaining acts; but also we incite and drive ourselves, God cooperating, to them. And so, he says, operating grace is that which makes us will to believe; because that is done in us, without us asking, and much less labouring and striving: And cooperating grace, that which makes us will to pray, to fast, and to give alms: because that is not done except by effort, and our industry cooperating. Whence he gathers that God does not work our willing without us; but only works that we will without us: since namely, we cooperate with God by willing, that is, freely producing the act of willing; but we do not cooperate by making that we will. Because we do not ourselves move and incite ourselves to willing: but he alone by internal inspiration moves and drives us.
pass_b: Thesis LII. In his view the grace needed for the will's later acts, after the first, is called cooperating, because once we have begun to turn to God we not only produce the later acts through free choice with God's help, but also spur and drive ourselves to them, with God cooperating.

'So operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that makes us will to believe, since this happens in us without our asking for it, much less toiling and striving for it; and cooperating grace is the grace that makes us will to pray, fast and give alms, since this does not happen except with our effort and diligence cooperating.'

From this he concludes that God does not work our willing without us, but only works without us the fact that we will. For we cooperate with God in willing, that is, in freely producing the act of willing, but we do not cooperate in bringing it about that we will, because we do not ourselves move and spur ourselves to will; he alone moves and drives us by an inward inspiration.

sections.title: Estius: the first good movement and Paul's conversion
sections.pass_a: LIII. To the same comes what Estius teaches, that Operating grace is commonly said to work in us without us, since the first act of conversion, or the first good motion of the will, which is the effect of that grace, is indeed from the will, as from an active and free principle; but yet God works it through his grace, without another previous motion of the will in us, by which we strive toward that first motion, or aspire, or by which the will commands it to itself. Since sometimes to a man, even greatly resisting, a good affection of the will is inspired, as happened in Paul. Whose conversion, as far as pertains to that change from evil into good made through operating grace, is the form and exemplar of the conversion of all sinners. Since through the grace of God from averse ones they are converted and from unwilling are made willing. But the remaining acts of the will, which follow that first, and by which we go on to cleave to God, the grace of God indeed works also in us; but yet our will already converted to God, not only produces them freely, but also through other prior acts commands them to itself. And so in a certain singular way it cooperates with divine grace, which therefore in this respect is called cooperating. On 2 Sent. Dist. 26 sect. 11.
pass_b: Thesis LIII. Estius's teaching comes to the same. Operating grace, he says, is commonly said to work in us without us because the first act of conversion, the first good movement of the will, which is the effect of that grace, does indeed come from the will as from an active and free source. Yet God works it by his grace without any earlier movement of the will in us by which we strive or aspire toward that first movement, or by which the will commands it of itself.

Indeed a good disposition of the will is sometimes breathed into a person even while he strongly resists, as happened with Paul. His conversion, as regards that change from evil to good brought about by operating grace, is the pattern and model for the conversion of all sinners, since by God's grace they are turned from being averse and made willing from being unwilling.

The later acts of the will that follow that first one, by which we go on clinging to God, are also worked in us by God's grace. But our will, now turned to God, not only produces them freely but also commands them of itself through other earlier acts.
In this way it cooperates with divine grace in a special manner, and for this reason the grace is called cooperating in this respect (on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, section 11).

sections.title: Jansenius: operating grace makes the first good will
sections.pass_a: LIV. In a not unlike way Jansenius Bishop of Ypres explains Operating and cooperating grace. Operating grace, he says, is that which alone without effort, without prayer, without merit of man preceding, works the will, or willing, by which the will from bad becomes good, and from unjust just. But Cooperating that which cooperates with man already willing, and striving, by increasing and strengthening that will to be firm, that he may effect and perfect what he has willed and strives for. And in the same place from Augustine he teaches that operating grace is that, by which when before we did not will, it is brought about that we will: cooperating, by which when we already will in act, it is brought about that we will more strongly, so that by overcoming any obstacles, we also do it in deed. That works that in any way we have good will, or willing good: this that that good will may be increased and strengthened. Whence he gathers that cooperating grace is never spoken in respect of the first good will, when the power of the will breaks out into it, since that first will, or good volition, is the effect of operating grace alone, but only in respect of good will after man has already begun to will, that that willing may persevere, be increased, and be heaped with good works as with fruits.
pass_b: Thesis LIV. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains operating and cooperating grace in much the same way. 'Operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that by itself, with no prior effort, prayer or merit on man's part, works the will, or the willing, by which the will is made good from bad and just from unjust.

Cooperating grace is the grace that cooperates with a man who already wills and strives, by enlarging that will and strengthening it to firmness, so that he may accomplish and complete what he has willed and is striving for.'

In the same place he teaches from Augustine that operating grace is the grace by which, when we did not will before, we are brought to will; and cooperating grace the grace by which, when we already actually will, we are brought to will more strongly, so that by overcoming every obstacle we also actually do it. The first works so that we have a good will, a willing of good, in some way or other; the second, so that this good will may be enlarged and strengthened.

From this he concludes that cooperating grace is never spoken of with respect to the first good will, when the will's power breaks out into it, since that first will, or good volition, is the effect of operating grace alone. It is spoken of only with respect to good will after a person has begun to will, so that this willing may last, grow and be enriched with good works as with fruit.

sections.title: Jansenius: no merit before the first good will; cooperating grace and growth
sections.pass_a: LV. Operating grace therefore, as he diligently observes, alone effects the first good will in man, not because man does not at the same time flow into that will, that is, into the motion of the will and consent, but because grace works that motion, we contributing nothing to having it, by asking, desiring, studying, meditating, and so bringing nothing at all of good merit, in respect of that will. For that is impossible, by the very fact by which it is laid down, to be the first good will, to which one is converted from a bad. In turn cooperating grace is so called, because it works something in us not alone, but with us at the same time cooperating; not by simultaneous influx only, by which we also cooperate with operating grace, but previously to the effect of that grace, by Willing, believing, desiring, asking, knocking, busying, and so even meriting; so that the effect of that cooperating grace is the whole increase of that first good will, up to the summit of human perfection. pass_b: Thesis LV. Operating grace, then, as he carefully observes, alone produces the first good will in a person. This is not because the person does not at the same time contribute his own influence to that will, that is, to the will's movement and consent, but because grace works that movement while we contribute nothing toward having it, whether by asking, desiring, striving or meditating, and so bring no good merit whatever with respect to that will.
Such merit is impossible, he says, for the very reason that this is laid down to be the first good will, to which one turns from a bad will.

Cooperating grace, in turn, is so called because it works something in us not alone but with us cooperating at the same time. It does so not merely by a simultaneous influence, by which we cooperate with operating grace too, but ahead of that grace's effect, by willing, believing, desiring, asking, knocking, taking pains and so even meriting.
Thus the effect of cooperating grace is the whole growth of that first good will, up to the height of human perfection (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 4, chapter 15).

sections.title: Alvarez: both graces in every devout work, by physical predetermination
sections.pass_a: LVI. From all these differs the opinion of Diego Alvarez. For he thinks that to any pious operation, whether it be interior, or exterior; whether it be that first by which we are converted to God, or any other following it, there always concur operating grace, and cooperating grace. And indeed operating grace is that, by which God Physically predetermines our will to consent in any good work: but cooperating, that by which God works any pious action with us. For both are necessary, both that God premove our free choice Physically and efficiently to any supernatural act; and that he concur with the same free choice, which already premoved by God moves itself to the good work. But operating grace is called in order to the first effect, in respect of which our will holds itself only, as moved: but cooperating, in order to the second, in which, moved, it moves itself. And this since our will in order to the previous motion, by which it is moved by God to supernatural acts, holds itself passively, since such motion is not produced actively by our free choice, but only by God, from whom is that help of operating grace. And again the will moved by God produces actively and freely supernatural operations, with the grace of God concurring. And therefore the grace of God, in that former respect, works without us: but in the latter we cooperate with it. On the Helps of divine grace book 9 Disp. 81.
pass_b: Thesis LVI. Diego Alvarez's view differs from all of these. He holds that in every devout work, whether inward or outward, whether it is the first by which we turn to God or any later one, operating and cooperating grace always both take part.

Operating grace is the grace by which God physically predetermines our will to consent to any good work; cooperating grace is the grace by which God works any devout action together with us. Both are needed: God must premove our free choice physically and efficiently to any supernatural act, and he must also act together with that same free choice, which, once premoved by God, moves itself to the good work.

Grace is called operating with regard to the first effect, in relation to which our will is only moved; and cooperating with regard to the second, in which the will, having been moved, moves itself. This is because our will is passive toward the prior motion by which God moves it to supernatural acts, since that motion is produced not actively by our free choice but by God alone, from whom that help of operating grace comes.

The will, moved by God, then actively and freely produces supernatural works, with God's grace acting together with it. So in the first respect God's grace works without us, and in the second we cooperate with it (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 9, disputation 81).

sections.title: How operating differs from rousing grace: the Jesuit answer
sections.pass_a: LVII. Here however the Doctors of the Roman Church ask, how operating Grace is distinguished from rousing: and cooperating grace from helping grace. But from what has already been said it can easily be gathered what should be answered to this question, according to the tenets of each one. For those who, with Vasquez, Molina, and most Jesuits, by rousing grace understand only Knocking and Soliciting grace, and indeed often in vain: but by Helping grace, that by which God concurs with special help with free choice, while it consents to grace, and obeys it: And again by operating grace, that which effects in us pious thoughts, and undeliberated motions, to which we concur Physically indeed, but not freely; but by cooperating, that which produces in us free acts of the will, by which we respond to God calling and inviting; those, I say, think that operating grace is the same as rousing, and helping grace the same as cooperating. Namely according to them, the same grace, is both called rousing, insofar as through holy thoughts, and pious desires sent into us it solicits and rouses us to good; And operating, insofar as it works these in us, without us freely concurring, and consenting. And similarly the same grace is both called helping, insofar as it helps us, while we consent to grace inviting; And cooperating, insofar as it does not work without us freely giving our consent.
pass_b: Thesis LVII. Here the doctors of the Roman Church raise the question how operating grace differs from rousing grace, and cooperating grace from assisting grace. From what has been said it is easy to work out how each party must answer, according to its own positions.

Some, with Vasquez, Molina and most of the Jesuits, take rousing grace to mean only the grace that knocks and urges, and that indeed often in vain; assisting grace, the grace by which God concurs by special help with free choice while free choice consents to grace and obeys it; operating grace, the grace that produces in us devout thoughts and undeliberate movements, in which we take part physically but not freely; and cooperating grace, the grace that produces in us the free acts of the will by which we answer God when he calls and invites.

These people hold that operating grace is the same as rousing grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace. For them one and the same grace is called rousing insofar as it urges and rouses us to good through the holy thoughts and devout desires it puts into us, and operating insofar as it works these in us without our freely concurring and consenting.

Likewise one and the same grace is called assisting insofar as it helps us while we consent to grace's invitation, and cooperating insofar as it does not work without us, as we freely give our consent.

sections.title: The same identification for Jansenius and Estius
sections.pass_a: LVIII. In the same way rousing grace is the same as operating, and helping grace the same as cooperating, for all those, who with Jansenius and Estius by rousing grace understand that, which really rouses the sinner from the sleep of sin, and by helping that by which man is helped, that he may perfect the good which he has already begun to will: And by operating that which effects in us the first act of conversion, by cooperating that which effects the others following, to which we cooperate not only by a certain free influx of the will, but also by some previous effort and striving of ours.
pass_b: Thesis LVIII. Rousing grace is likewise the same as operating grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace, for all who, with Jansenius and Estius, take rousing grace to be the grace that actually wakes the sinner from the sleep of sin, and assisting grace the grace by which a person is helped to complete the good he has already begun to will.

They also take operating grace to be the grace that produces in us the first act of conversion, and cooperating grace the grace that produces the acts that follow, in which we cooperate not only by a free contribution of the will but also by some prior effort and striving of our own.

sections.title: Bellarmine's mixed view: rousing grace is wider than operating
sections.pass_a: LIX. But those who, with Jansenius and Estius, will indeed that operating grace is called, that which works in us the first conversion; and cooperating, that which moves us to the good works which thence follow: but maintain with the Jesuits that rousing grace is, that by which we are knocked that we may wake from the sleep of vices, even if by our fault we often remain asleep; but helping that which strengthens and helps us, while we really shake off that sleep: those, I say, like Bellarmine, distinguish rousing grace from operating, and consequently helping grace from cooperating: For to them rousing grace extends more widely than operating. And so they divide rousing grace into sufficient and efficacious. And again efficacious into operating and cooperating, as may be seen in the same Bellarmine book 1 on Grace already often cited.
pass_b: Thesis LIX. Others agree with Jansenius and Estius that operating grace is the grace that works the first conversion in us, and cooperating grace the grace that moves us to the good works that follow from it.

But they maintain with the Jesuits that rousing grace is the grace by which we are knocked at so that we may wake from the sleep of vice, even if through our own fault we often stay asleep, and assisting grace the grace that strengthens and helps us while we actually shake off that sleep.

These, like Bellarmine, distinguish rousing grace from operating grace, and so assisting grace from cooperating grace, since for them rousing grace covers more ground than operating grace. They therefore divide rousing grace into sufficient and efficacious, and efficacious grace again into operating and cooperating, as may be seen in Bellarmine, book 1 On Grace, already cited many times.

sections.title: Alvarez: rousing grace is sufficient, operating grace efficacious
sections.pass_a: LX. Similarly Alvarez distinguishes rousing grace from operating: since rousing grace to him is a certain grace drawing and alluring the will to good only morally. But operating, a grace not only morally, but also physically premoving and predetermining the will to good. And so, according to him, rousing grace is the same as sufficient grace. But operating and cooperating grace pertain to efficacious grace.
pass_b: Thesis LX. Alvarez likewise distinguishes rousing grace from operating grace. For him rousing grace is a grace that draws and attracts the will toward good only morally, while operating grace not only morally but also physically premoves and predetermines the will toward good.
So on his view rousing grace is the same as sufficient grace, whereas operating and cooperating grace belong to efficacious grace.

sections.title: The chief dispute: is assisting grace prior in nature? (Jesuits)
sections.pass_a: LXI. But among the Theologians of the Roman School the chief controversy here is about the way in which the grace of God cooperates with our will. For the Jesuits, and very many other Doctors of the Roman School, deny that helping, or cooperating grace concurs to the supernatural work prior in nature, than free choice; And this so as not to admit, that grace predetermines free choice. Whence, in their judgment, the freedom of the will would perish; on which, from that hypothesis, divine grace would impose some necessity of acting, which could not stand with freedom. So among others thinks and reasons Peter of Saint Joseph, in the idea of speculative Theology, book four, chapter six, where his third Resolution thus begins, Helping grace does not concur prior in nature to the supernatural work, than free choice.
pass_b: Thesis LXI. Among the theologians of the Roman school, however, the main dispute here concerns the way in which God's grace cooperates with our will.

The Jesuits and many other doctors of the Roman school deny that assisting or cooperating grace concurs in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature. They do so in order not to admit that grace predetermines free choice, since in their judgment the freedom of the will would then perish: on that supposition divine grace would lay on the will some necessity of acting that could not stand with freedom.

Peter of Saint Joseph, among others, thinks and argues this way in his Idea theologiae speculativae, book 4, chapter 6, where his third resolution begins: 'Assisting grace does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature.'

lemmas.gloss: deny that helping, or cooperating grace concurs to the supernatural work prior in nature

lemmas.latin: Et hoc ne admittant, gratiam praedeterminare liberum arbitrium

The print reads 'Der gratia' and, in the quoted resolution, 'uon concurrit'; the lock keeps both, and the English follows the evident 'Dei' (of God) and 'non' (not).

sections.title: Alvarez: assisting grace prior in the order of causality
sections.pass_a: LXII. But on the contrary others maintain that helping and cooperating grace, according to the order of causality, goes before free choice, and acts before it: And although at the same time in time both grace, and free choice flow into the pious operation, yet the influx of grace is in a certain way prior in nature, and not simultaneous in order of causality with the influx of free choice. This is the opinion of Diego Alvarez in the Epitome on the Helps of divine grace, book three, chapter nineteen, whose heading is this, That cooperating Grace, insofar as cooperating, is prevenient, or premoving free choice to consent, and not only equally, and simultaneously with it flowing into the pious operation. But the same chapter begins with these words, From the premises it is established, that cooperating grace, insofar as it is distinguished from rousing, is prevenient to the free cooperation of created choice, not indeed by priority of time, but of reason only and of causality.
pass_b: Thesis LXII. Others, on the contrary, maintain that assisting and cooperating grace comes before free choice in the order of causality and acts before it does. Although grace and free choice act on the devout work at the same time, the influence of grace is in some way prior in nature, and is not simultaneous with the influence of free choice in the order of causality.

This is the view of Diego Alvarez in the Epitome of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 3, chapter 19, whose heading is: 'That cooperating grace, as cooperating, is prevenient, or premoves free choice to consent, and does not merely act on the devout work equally and simultaneously with it.'

The chapter itself begins: 'From what has been laid down it is clear that cooperating grace, insofar as it is distinguished from rousing grace, goes before the free cooperation of created choice, not by priority in time but only in reason and causality.'

sections.title: Freedom kept: the power to act otherwise in the divided sense
sections.pass_a: LXIII. Nor on that account do they think anything is prejudiced to the freedom of the human will; since the grace of God so moves and determines created free choice to act, that it does not take from it the power of acting otherwise: so that grace being posited, it acts indeed infallibly, but always in the divided sense it is able not to act, or to act otherwise.
pass_b: Thesis LXIII. They do not think this harms the freedom of the human will in any way. God's grace moves and determines created free choice to act in such a way that it does not remove its power to act otherwise.
So when grace is given, the will does act without fail, yet in the divided sense it always remains able not to act or to act otherwise.

sections.title: Molinists: assisting grace only a partial cause
sections.pass_a: LXIV. Moreover those who follow the Method and doctrine of Molina the Jesuit, teach that helping, or cooperating grace does not hold itself properly as total cause, in respect of the supernatural act, but as partial cause only. And this because helping grace, in their opinion, does not produce the supernatural act, except dependently on Free choice.
pass_b: Thesis LXIV. Further, those who follow the method and teaching of the Jesuit Molina hold that assisting or cooperating grace is not, strictly, the total cause of the supernatural act, but only a partial cause.
Their reason is that, in their view, assisting grace produces the supernatural act only in dependence on free choice.

sections.title: Totality of effect, not of cause: the two horses
sections.pass_a: LXV. They admit indeed that the whole supernatural act depends on grace: but they add that it does not depend on it totally, but partially only: because grace, namely, cannot produce it, except dependently on the concurrence of the will. And therefore grace can indeed be called total cause of the good act by totality of effect, but not by totality of cause, of which here it is treated: since the whole effect indeed depends on grace, but yet as on a cause which does not produce it without another cause concurring, and acting together with it. Whence it is that they compare grace and free choice to two horses drawing the same chariot together, of which neither acts before the other, and moves the other to act, and which are only partial causes of that drawing; although the whole drawing can be said, to depend on each horse, because each contributes something to the whole drawing.
pass_b: Thesis LXV. They grant that the whole supernatural act depends on grace, but add that it depends on grace not totally but only in part, because grace cannot produce it except in dependence on the will's concurrence.

Grace can therefore be called the total cause of the good act by totality of effect, but not by totality of cause, which is the point at issue here. The whole effect does depend on grace, but as on a cause that does not produce it without another cause acting with it at the same time.

That is why they compare grace and free choice to two horses pulling the same cart together. Neither of them acts first and moves the other to act, and each is only a partial cause of the pulling, although the whole pulling can be said to depend on each horse, since each contributes something to all of it.

sections.title: On their view rousing grace imposes no necessity either
sections.pass_a: LXVI. And so in their mind, helping grace as such and precisely considered, does not move man to act, but helps him in the actual operation. But rousing grace, although it moves man to act, yet does not impose on him a necessity of acting; but leaves to him his parts, that namely he determine himself to the pious work, since otherwise he can abstain from it, if he will, and determine himself otherwise. Whence neither should it be called total cause, or adequate of the good operation, as may be seen in the same Peter of Saint Joseph in the place cited above.
pass_b: Thesis LXVI. On their view, then, assisting grace taken strictly and as such does not move a person to act, but helps him in the actual working.

Rousing grace, though it does move a person to act, does not lay on him any necessity of acting. It leaves him his own part to play, namely to determine himself to the devout work, since otherwise he can refrain from it, if he wishes, and determine himself differently.
So it too should not be called the total or adequate cause of the good work, as may be seen in the same Peter of Saint Joseph at the place cited above.
