sections.title: Estius and the recent Thomists: grace the total cause
sections.pass_a: LXVII. But on the contrary Estius and the more recent Thomists teach that the grace of God is so the total cause of the good work, that whatever of good is in the work it makes the whole, and the whole work is to be ascribed to divine grace, as to total cause, not only as to partial.
pass_b: Thesis LXVII. Estius and the more recent Thomists, by contrast, hold that God's grace is the total cause of a good work in such a way that it produces all the good there is in the work. The whole work must therefore be credited to divine grace as its total cause, and not merely as a partial one.

sections.title: Wholly from grace and wholly from free choice: subordinate causes
sections.pass_a: LXVIII. But although absolutely and properly speaking, they assert that the whole good work is from the grace of God, nevertheless they teach that the same good work is wholly from free choice also. Because nothing prevents something being wholly from two causes, of which one is subordinated to the other: so namely that the inferior cause receives all its power of operating, and all motion from the superior. And this they teach is perpetual in the first cause, and the second cause; whatever kind the second cause finally be, whether it act freely, or naturally, because, namely, it is necessary, that whatever is done by the second cause be referred to the first: Nor can in any way in these a partition of works be admitted: that something in any part of it be thought to be done by the second cause, which is not also wholly, and in every part done by the first cause applying the second cause to all its operation.
pass_b: Thesis LXVIII. Yet although, speaking absolutely and strictly, they assert that the whole good work comes from God's grace, they also teach that the same good work comes wholly from free choice as well.
Nothing prevents a thing from coming wholly from two causes when one is subordinate to the other, that is, when the lower cause receives all its power to act and all its motion from the higher.

This, they teach, always holds between the first cause and a second cause, whatever kind of second cause it may be and whether it acts freely or by nature, because whatever a second cause does must be traced back to the first.

Between these causes no division of the work can be admitted in any way, as if some part of it were thought to be done by the second cause that is not also done wholly, in every part, by the first cause, which applies the second cause to all its working.

sections.title: God makes man act, not the reverse
sections.pass_a: LXIX. They say therefore that the whole good is accomplished at once and by an undivided work by grace and free choice: nor is that distinct which is from free choice, and that which is from grace; because that is not distinct which is from the first cause, and that which is from the second cause. But between each agent they teach that this is the difference, that free choice, as it has its being from God, so also has all this that it works well from the grace of God, working in it, and through it: but not on the contrary, either in whole, or in part, does God in that which he works, depend on the free choice of man. For God makes that man makes, but man does not make that God makes. Which same reason is in every work, or action, which is done by any second cause whatever. And so according to these Doctors, divine grace, and free choice do not cooperate as partial causes, which in acting depend on each other, but as total and subordinate causes, of which the inferior depends on and is moved by the superior, not conversely. As may be seen more widely in the same Estius on 2 Sent. dist. 26 paragr. 29.
pass_b: Thesis LXIX. They therefore say that the whole good is carried out by grace and free choice together, in one undivided work. What comes from free choice is not distinct from what comes from grace, just as what comes from the first cause is not distinct from what comes from the second.

Between the two agents, they teach, the difference is this: as free choice has its being from God, so it has all its good working from God's grace, which works in it and through it; but God, in what he works, does not in turn depend on man's free choice, either wholly or in part. For God causes man to act; man does not cause God to act.
The same holds in every work or action done by any second cause whatever.

So on the view of these doctors divine grace and free choice do not cooperate as partial causes that depend on each other in acting, but as total causes ordered one under the other, the lower depending on the higher and moved by it, not the reverse. This may be seen at more length in the same Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 29.

sections.title: Prevenient and subsequent, leading and accompanying; sufficient and efficacious deferred
sections.pass_a: LXX. Further with the divisions of grace already brought coincide certain others, which differ little or nothing from them. As when grace is divided into prevenient grace and into subsequent grace: and into leading and accompanying. For by leading and prevenient grace Theologians understand that same which they call rousing and operating: and by accompanying or subsequent grace, that which elsewhere is called helping, or cooperating. For that grace which rouses us to good, and so far works in us without us, the same also goes before us: but that which helps us in the actual operation, and cooperates with us, the same is thought to accompany our wills in acting well, and follows that former grace. Some however seek certain subtle differences between these divisions of grace, which to relate and mention does not much serve our purpose. What chiefly remains to be considered here, is that celebrated division of grace into sufficient and efficacious: but because the accurate exposition of it is a matter of longer inquiry, it has seemed good to defer it to the next disputation.
pass_b: Thesis LXX. Some other divisions of grace coincide with those already given and differ little or not at all from them, as when grace is divided into prevenient and subsequent, and into leading and accompanying.

By leading and prevenient grace the theologians mean the same grace they call rousing and operating, and by accompanying or subsequent grace the grace otherwise called assisting or cooperating. The grace that rouses us to good, and to that extent works in us without us, also goes before us; the grace that helps us in the actual working and cooperates with us is held to accompany our wills in doing good, and comes after that first grace.
Some, however, look for certain subtle distinctions among these divisions of grace, but recounting and mentioning them would not do much for our purpose.

What chiefly remains to be considered here is the well-known division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. But since a careful account of it calls for a longer inquiry, it has seemed best to put it off to the next disputation.
